note: Every Grafana dashboard in apps/*/ and infrastructure/auth/ is rendered from this file by scripts/render_namespace_dashboard.py. See docs/dashboards.md. `services` are pod-name prefixes in that namespace; a `pvc` ending in -* is a CNPG cluster whose instance number changes on switchover.

dashboards.title: arr-stack — Sonarr / Radarr / Prowlarr / Bazarr / Jellyfin

panels.title: Node package power (RAPL)
panels.description: Package power drawn by the CPU that hosts the GPU, from node-exporter's Intel RAPL counters in watts. The GPU has no exporter of its own any more, so the node-side reading is what tracks how hard the embedding workload is working.

panels.title: Node thermal zones
panels.description: Temperature of every node thermal zone in degrees Celsius. A model that keeps the GPU busy shows up here as a sustained rise before it shows up as latency.

panels.title: Consolidation backlog
panels.description: Facts waiting in the consolidation queue for the selected tenant. A backlog that only grows means the extractor cannot keep up with what the agents retain.

panels.title: Drain rate (facts/hour)
panels.description: How fast the consolidation backlog shrinks over the last hour, in facts per hour. Negative is draining, positive means the queue is growing.

panels.title: Operations/sec
panels.description: Retain, recall and reflect operations per second across the selected tenants — the request load the memory service is absorbing.

panels.title: Retain/sec
panels.description: Memory retain operations per second. A retain that stalls shows up here first, before the backlog grows.

panels.title: Recall/sec
panels.description: Memory recall (search) operations per second. This is the read path every agent session hits.

panels.title: Reflect/sec
panels.description: Reflect (synthesis) operations per second. Reflect is the expensive path: it re-reads memory rather than one bank lookup.

panels.title: Backlog over time
panels.description: Consolidation backlog per tenant over the selected range. A rising line is the earliest signal that extraction is falling behind.

panels.title: Pending / processing operations
panels.description: Async operations still pending or in flight, by operation type and status. Stuck processing counts are a wedged worker.

panels.title: Operations per second by type
panels.description: Retain, recall and reflect throughput split by operation, so one slow path cannot hide behind the total.

panels.title: p95 latency by operation type
panels.description: 95th percentile server-side latency per operation type in seconds. Recall rising alone points at the vector store, reflect at the LLM.

panels.title: Operations per second by bank
panels.description: Operation throughput per memory bank. One hot bank is usually one noisy agent session rather than a service-wide load change.

panels.title: Requests/sec
panels.description: HTTP requests per second served by the Hindsight API. The API is what agents and the MCP bridge call; a collapse here means memory is unavailable.

panels.title: Requests in progress
panels.description: HTTP requests currently being served. A number that only grows is a stuck pool or a hung dependency.

panels.title: Error rate (5xx)
panels.description: Share of HTTP requests answered with a 5xx over the last five minutes. Above one percent the API is failing its callers.

panels.title: p95 latency
panels.description: 95th percentile HTTP latency in seconds. Agents block on this call, so it is the memory path's contribution to session latency.

panels.title: Requests/sec by endpoint
panels.description: HTTP request rate split by endpoint. Retain and recall volumes diverge when a client changes its memory strategy.

panels.title: HTTP latency percentiles
panels.description: p50, p95 and p99 HTTP latency in seconds. The gap between p50 and p99 is the tail a slow database query hides in.

panels.title: Error rate over time
panels.description: 5xx and 4xx share of HTTP requests over time. 5xx is the service breaking; a 4xx spike is usually one client sending bad queries.

panels.title: DB pool size
panels.description: Connections the API currently holds in its Postgres pool. At the maximum the API queues requests instead of serving them.

panels.title: Idle connections
panels.description: Idle connections in the API's Postgres pool. Zero idle with a large pool means every connection is stuck on a slow query.

panels.title: Active connections
panels.description: Connections the pool reports as in use (size minus idle). Sustained saturation points at the database, not the API.

panels.title: Pool utilisation
panels.description: Share of the maximum Postgres pool in use. Above eighty percent the API starts waiting on the connection pool.

panels.title: Memory (RSS max)
panels.description: Resident memory of the API process in bytes. Near the container limit the pod is one allocation away from an OOMKill.

panels.title: Active threads
panels.description: Threads inside the API process. A count that climbs and never falls is a leaked worker pool.

panels.title: Open file descriptors
panels.description: File descriptors held by the API process. Descriptors climbing toward the limit is a socket or log-file leak.

panels.title: Total CPU time
panels.description: Cumulative CPU seconds the API process has burned. The slope of this line is the process CPU rate.

panels.title: Connection pool over time
panels.description: Pool size, idle, active and maximum connections over time. Active pinned at maximum while idle stays zero is pool exhaustion.

panels.title: Memory usage over time
panels.description: Resident memory of the API process over time. A sawtooth that returns to the same floor is normal; a rising floor is a leak.

panels.title: CPU usage rate (seconds/second)
panels.description: User and system CPU time per second consumed by the API process. One full core reads as 1.0.

panels.title: Threads and file descriptors over time
panels.description: Thread and file-descriptor counts over time. Both should drift flat; a rising line is a resource leak.

panels.title: Total LLM calls
panels.description: LLM calls the extractor has made for the selected tenants. This is the spend the memory service generates on the model lane.

panels.title: Total tokens used
panels.description: Input plus output tokens the extractor has spent. Tokens, not calls, is what the free-tier limits and the bill are measured in.

panels.title: Input tokens
panels.description: Prompt tokens sent to the extraction model. A jump without more calls means bigger prompts (more context per fact).

panels.title: Output tokens
panels.description: Completion tokens the extraction model returned. Output is the expensive half on most providers.

panels.title: LLM calls per second by scope
panels.description: LLM call rate split by extraction scope. Each scope is a prompt shape, so one scope storming is one prompt getting more work.

panels.title: Token usage rate (tokens/sec)
panels.description: Input and output tokens per second across the selected tenants — the rate the model lane has to sustain.

panels.title: LLM call latency p95 by scope
panels.description: 95th percentile extraction call latency in seconds per scope. Latency here sets how fast the consolidation backlog drains.

panels.title: Token usage by scope (tokens/sec)
panels.description: Token rate split by extraction scope, so a single expensive prompt cannot hide inside the total.

panels.title: Excalidraw available replicas
panels.description: Available replicas of the excalidraw Deployment in apps-whiteboard. Below one the editor has no backend and the public page fails.

panels.title: Tunnel connectors available
panels.description: Available replicas of the cloudflared-whiteboard tunnel. The pod runs in apps-tldraw because the Cloudflare route is pinned to a service there; below one connector the public hostname returns CF error 1033.

panels.title: Probes succeeding
panels.description: hostwatch_probe_success is 1 per configured target while the last probe passed, so a drop here is the exact set of endpoints that went dark.

panels.title: Heartbeat age
panels.description: Seconds since the watchdog last received a heartbeat from the host it watches. HostWatchHeartbeatMissing fires on the same series, so a rising line is the alert before the alert.

panels.title: Heartbeat rejections (24h)
panels.description: Heartbeats the watchdog accepted the connection for but refused, which is what a mis-scoped token or a clock skew looks like from the inside.

panels.title: Consecutive probe failures
panels.description: Per-target failure count straight from hostwatch_probe_consecutive_failures. HostWatchProbeFailing pages at 3, so this panel shows how close each target is to that line.

panels.title: Probe duration by target
panels.description: How long each watched endpoint took to answer, from hostwatch_probe_duration_seconds. A slow probe is a degraded dependency before it is a down one.

dashboards.title: karakeep — Bookmarks, search and AI tagging

panels.title: Backup age
panels.description: Hours since karakeep-backup last succeeded, from kube_cronjob_status_last_successful_time. KarakeepBackupStale pages at 30 hours, so this is the same clock the alert reads.

panels.title: Replicas ready
panels.description: Ready replicas against the requested count for every Deployment in the namespace, so a wedged rollout shows as ready below desired instead of a green dashboard.

panels.title: Failed jobs (6h)
panels.description: Jobs in the namespace that ended in Failed, which is the backup and maintenance half of the golden signals that no HTTP metric covers.

dashboards.title: openchamber — Workspaces, sync and the agent runner

panels.title: Memory against limit
panels.description: Working set of the whole namespace as a percentage of its memory limits. OpenChamberMemoryAbove85PercentLimit pages on the same ratio, per pod.

panels.title: Workspace volume used
panels.description: Used space on the openchamber-data claim as a percentage of its capacity. The NFS export behind it is shared with the host, so a leak here fills a disk the host also writes to.

panels.title: Restarts by container
panels.description: Container restarts in the namespace over the last hour. The agent runner and the syncthing sidecar are the two that restart without taking the web pod down.

dashboards.title: riffradar — Demo app, backups and restarts

panels.title: Backup age
panels.description: Hours since riffradar-backup last succeeded. RiffRadarBackupStale pages on this series, and the app exports no /metrics of its own, so the backup is the only liveness signal with a schedule.

panels.title: Replicas ready
panels.description: Ready replicas against the requested count for every Deployment in the namespace. RiffRadarPodNotReady excludes Job-owned pods, so this is the same population the alert judges.

panels.title: Restarts per hour
panels.description: Container restarts in the namespace over the last hour. RiffRadarRestartLoop fires from this same counter, so a non-zero line is the leading edge of that page.

dashboards.title: Observability — SLOs
dashboards.description: SLOs and error budgets for Open WebUI, Hindsight API and Grafana, generated from scripts/dashboards/manifest.json.

dashboards.title: Observability — Pipeline health
dashboards.description: The telemetry pipeline itself: what the OpenTelemetry Collector accepts, exports and fails to send, how full its queue is, and whether the components behind it are up. Generated from scripts/dashboards/manifest.json.
dashboards.overview: Where telemetry is lost. The receiver counters are what applications hand the collector; the exporter counters are what actually reaches Loki, Tempo and Prometheus. A board that is green on pod readiness and red here is the failure class this dashboard exists for: every pod is ready and the data still stops.

services.label: prometheus
services.cpuDescription: CPU used by the prometheus pod next to its request and limit, in cores. The pod sets no CPU limit (only a memory limit), so the limit series is expected to stay empty rather than being a defect.

panels.title: Telemetry accepted per second
panels.description: Collector receiver throughput by signal, from otelcol_receiver_accepted_spans, _metric_points and _log_records. These counters carry no _total suffix on the :8888 scrape endpoint.

panels.title: Telemetry exported per second
panels.description: Collector exporter throughput by signal, from otelcol_exporter_sent_*. Compare with the accepted panel: a widening gap is data the pipeline took and did not deliver.

panels.title: Export failures per second
panels.description: Rate of otelcol_exporter_send_failed_*, the batch the collector dropped for good. Any sustained non-zero value here means the backends are rejecting or unreachable.

panels.title: Exporter queue fill
panels.description: otelcol_exporter_queue_size as a percentage of otelcol_exporter_queue_capacity. This is the one number that says the collector is falling behind before it starts dropping batches.

panels.title: Receiver throughput by signal
panels.description: Per-signal receiver throughput on a timeline, so a single exporter failing does not hide behind the sum of the other two.

panels.title: Exporter throughput by signal
panels.description: Per-signal exporter throughput on a timeline. Read it against the receiver panel above it: the two lines should track each other.

panels.title: Exporter send failures
panels.description: Failed exports per second over time, split by signal, so a backend outage is visible as a shape rather than a single number.

panels.title: Exporter queue depth vs capacity
panels.description: Queue size and capacity as two lines. Capacity is flat, so the gap closing is the collector running out of headroom.

panels.title: Refused telemetry per second
panels.description: otelcol_receiver_refused_*: data the collector rejected before it ever reached a queue. Memory limits and malformed batches both show up here.

panels.title: Collector process memory
panels.description: otelcol_process_memory_rss for the collector. The queue lives in memory, so this is the ceiling that turns a slow backend into dropped data.

panels.title: Backend pods ready
panels.description: Ready pods behind the pipeline: Loki, Tempo and Prometheus. When this drops, the export failure panels above are the symptom and this is the cause.

dashboards.title: Homelab — Flux reconciliation and nodes
dashboards.description: GitOps health for the cluster: flux controller reconciliations, stuck HelmReleases and Kustomizations, and the node pressure underneath them. Generated from scripts/dashboards/manifest.json.
dashboards.overview: Does the cluster still converge? Reconciliation rate and duration are on top, stuck objects next, then node CPU, memory and disk. A dashboard that is green on application pods and red here means main is merged and not applied.

panels.title: Flux pod restarts (5m)
panels.description: Controller restarts in flux-system over five minutes. A controller that restarts silently stops reconciling, which looks identical to a quiet cluster.

panels.title: Flux reconciliations per minute
panels.description: gotk_reconcile_duration_seconds_count as a per-minute rate: how much work the controllers are actually doing.

panels.title: Stuck HelmReleases
panels.description: HelmReleases reporting ready=False in gotk_resource_info. Each one is a release that will not converge until someone looks.

panels.title: Stuck Kustomizations
panels.description: Kustomizations reporting ready=False. This is the count that explains why a merged manifest never reached the cluster.

panels.title: Reconcile duration p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: Quantiles of gotk_reconcile_duration_seconds by kind. Reconciling is allowed to be slow; growing slowly forever is how a cluster falls behind main.

panels.title: Controller CPU against limit
panels.description: Controller CPU usage next to the limit it is allowed, from kube_pod_container_resource_limits. A controller throttled at its limit reconciles late, not never.

panels.title: Node status
panels.description: Nodes reporting Ready against the number of nodes the API server knows about.

panels.title: Node CPU utilisation
panels.description: Idle CPU inverted, per instance, from node-exporter. The pressure that makes every controller above slow at once.

panels.title: Node memory utilisation
panels.description: Memory in use per instance on the timeline. Higher memory delays every reconcile without failing any of them.

dashboards.title: Homelab — Power and thermals
dashboards.description: What the homelab host is doing to its own silicon: package temperature, RAPL power draw, thermal zones and fans from node-exporter. Generated from scripts/dashboards/manifest.json.
dashboards.overview: Thermals and power for the physical host. Temperatures and fan speeds come from node-exporter hwmon and thermal zones, draw from the RAPL energy counters. Rising package power at flat temperature is work; flat power at rising temperature is airflow.

panels.title: CPU package temperature
panels.description: The coretemp package sensor from node_hwmon_temp_celsius. This is the number that decides whether the host throttles.

panels.title: CPU package power
panels.description: RAPL package energy converted to watts. The same series the existing power board has always reported, now generated.

panels.title: Hottest sensor
panels.description: Maximum of every hwmon temperature on the host, so a single hot sensor cannot hide behind an average.

panels.title: Thermal zones
panels.description: ACPI thermal zone temperatures, which on this host is where the NVMe and board sensors show up.

panels.title: Fan speeds
panels.description: node_hwmon_fan_rpm per fan. A fan reading zero at high package temperature is the failure this board exists to catch.

panels.title: Load average
panels.description: node_load1 for the host. Work is what makes power draw go up, so this is the explanation for the panels above.

panels.title: Memory utilisation
panels.description: Memory in use on the host. Sustained high memory is the other half of load: it is why a machine that is idle on CPU is still doing work.

panels.title: Filesystem utilisation
panels.description: Used space per mountpoint, tmpfs and overlay excluded. A full disk raises the temperature of nothing and breaks everything.

dashboards.title: Homelab — System load and pressure
dashboards.description: Host and pod pressure in one place: load, CPU, memory, disk I/O, network and the busiest containers by CPU and memory. Generated from scripts/dashboards/manifest.json.
dashboards.overview: Which resource is short. Host load, CPU, memory and disk first, then the containers responsible for it. Every panel is derived, not hand-written: re-rendering reproduces this file byte for byte.

panels.title: Load average per host
panels.description: node_load1 and node_load5 on the same axis. Load above the core count is a queue, and on this host the queue is usually disk rather than CPU.

panels.title: CPU utilisation per host
panels.description: Idle CPU inverted, per instance, from node-exporter. The same series node CPU alerts fire on.

panels.title: Memory used per host
panels.description: Memory in use per instance from MemAvailable against MemTotal. Swap pressure starts well before this reaches 100.

panels.title: Filesystem used per mountpoint
panels.description: Used space per mountpoint, tmpfs and overlay excluded. The homelab has several NFS exports, so the mountpoint label is the whole story.

panels.title: Disk I/O utilisation
panels.description: Percentage of wall time each device spent serving I/O. This is usually the real explanation for load on this host.

panels.title: Network receive per interface
panels.description: Inbound bytes per second per physical interface. veth and loopback are excluded so container churn does not dominate the graph.

panels.title: Network transmit per interface
panels.description: Outbound bytes per second per physical interface, same exclusions as the receive panel.

panels.title: Top pods by CPU
panels.description: The ten containers using the largest share of their CPU limit, from container_cpu_usage_seconds_total against kube_pod_container_resource_limits. Expressed against the limit so a hot pod is comparable to a cold one.

targets.expr: topk(10, 100 * (sum by (namespace, pod) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{container!=""}[5m])) / sum by (namespace, pod) (kube_pod_container_resource_limits{resource="cpu",container!=""})))

panels.title: Top pods by memory
panels.description: The ten containers using the largest share of their memory limit. Memory pressure on this host comes from a handful of pods, not from the sum.

targets.expr: topk(10, 100 * (sum by (namespace, pod) (container_memory_working_set_bytes{container!=""}) / sum by (namespace, pod) (kube_pod_container_resource_limits{resource="memory",container!=""})))

panels.title: Nodes ready
panels.description: Nodes reporting Ready against the number of nodes the API server knows about.
